title: Idiomatic expressions
why: To understand Spaniards in everyday life and speak more naturally, the learner discovers about fifteen very common idioms (meter la pata, estar hecho polvo, costar un ojo de la cara…) and their English equivalents. It wraps up the unit “Culture and leisure” by reusing the past tenses, the subjunctive and pronouns.

{"lessons": ["

Body and head

Like English, Spanish loves images taken from the body. Some expressions are very close to ours, others are completely different. In each one, only the verb is conjugated: the rest never changes.

ExpressionLiterallyIn English
costar un ojo de la carato cost an eye from the faceto cost an arm and a leg
tomar el pelo a alguiento take someone's hairto pull someone's leg
no tener pelos en la lenguato have no hairs on your tonguenot to mince words
meter la patato put your paw into put your foot in it, to blow it
echar una manoto throw a handto lend a hand
no pegar ojonot to stick an eye shutnot to sleep a wink
en un abrir y cerrar de ojosin an opening and closing of eyesin the blink of an eye
Este piso cuesta un ojo de la cara.This apartment costs an arm and a leg.
¿Me estás tomando el pelo?Are you pulling my leg?
¿Me echas una mano con las maletas?Can you give me a hand with the suitcases?
Mi abuela no tiene pelos en la lengua.My grandmother doesn't mince words.

Different body parts, same idea: Spain pays with an eye (un ojo de la cara, just one!), English with an arm and a leg; Spain takes your hair, English pulls your leg. And meter la pata is exactly “putting your foot in it”: saying or doing the wrong thing.

", "

Tiredness, ease, success

ExpressionLiterallyIn English
estar hecho polvoto be turned to dustto be wiped out, exhausted
estar en las nubesto be in the cloudsto have your head in the clouds
ser pan comidoto be eaten breadto be a piece of cake
dar en el clavoto hit on the nailto hit the nail on the head
ponerse las pilasto put your batteries into get your act together, to buckle down
tirar la toallato throw the towelto throw in the towel
ser uña y carneto be nail and fleshto be joined at the hip, inseparable
estar como una cabrato be like a goatto be nuts (informal)
llover a cántarosto rain by the pitcherfulto rain cats and dogs, to pour
Después de la mudanza, estoy hecha polvo.After the move, I'm wiped out.
Este ejercicio es pan comido.This exercise is a piece of cake.
¡Has dado en el clavo!You've hit the nail on the head!
Si quieres aprobar, tienes que ponerte las pilas.If you want to pass, you need to buckle down.
Lucía y Marta son uña y carne desde el colegio.Lucía and Marta have been inseparable since school.

Estar en las nubes works just like English “to have your head in the clouds” (distracted, daydreaming). Don't confuse it with “on cloud nine” (very happy): for that, Spanish says estar en el séptimo cielo.

", "

Using them well

The verb is conjugated, the adjective agrees

These expressions behave in a sentence like any other verb: Ayer metí la pata, Me he puesto las pilas, Siempre me tomas el pelo. In estar hecho polvo, hecho agrees with the person:

SpanishEnglish
Javier está hecho polvo.Javier is wiped out.
Lucía está hecha polvo.Lucía is wiped out.
Mis padres están hechos polvo.My parents are wiped out.
Mis hermanas están hechas polvo.My sisters are wiped out.

Ser or estar?

The verb is part of the expression: ser pan comido, ser uña y carne, but estar en las nubes, estar hecho polvo, estar como una cabra. Always learn them with their verb.

To whom? The indirect pronoun

With tomar el pelo and echar una mano, the person involved is an indirect object: Me tomas el pelo (you're pulling my leg), Le eché una mano a mi vecina (I gave my neighbor a hand).

These expressions are informal, but everyone uses them, at any age. Just avoid them in a formal work email. And never translate an English idiom word for word: “it's raining cats and dogs” is llueve a cántaros, not “llueve gatos y perros.”
